lessons.title: Exponential change and graph features
lessons.objective: Distinguish multiplication from addition and interpret exponential factors, percentage change, transformations, domains, ranges, and asymptotes.
scope: Positive bases distinct from one for nonconstant real exponential functions
Integer powers and negative exponents as prerequisites
Equal-step ratios versus differences
Percentage factors and repeated change
Horizontal shifts, signed output scaling, offsets, monotonicity, and asymptotes
workedExamples: Compare 12,18,27 with 12,18,24 on equal input steps
A 20 percent decrease gives factor 4/5; after three steps 50 becomes 128/5
Evaluate 3^-2 exactly and distinguish negative exponents from negative results
For 2^(x-1)-3 find anchor (1,-2), domain R, range (-3,infinity), and horizontal asymptote -3
For -2(1/2)^x+5 explain increasing output, range below 5, and an unattained asymptote
lessons.guided: Given an equal-step table with initial value 8 and factor 3/2, recover the ratio, classify multiplicative change, and predict the next exact output.

interaction.purpose: Change initial value, factor, and offset; predict a second-step value and asymptote; compare an exponential curve with a linear model matching the first step and an exact labeled table.

mistakes: Treat percentage as the whole multiplier
Forget the unchanged portion
Write new=old+change before simplifying the factor.
Use the same additive increment every step
Confuse linear and multiplicative change
Compare ratios and differences over equal input intervals.
Include an asymptote in the output range
Confuse approaching with attaining
A positive exponential never equals zero at finite input.
Infer monotonicity only from the base
Ignore a negative outside coefficient
Track the output reflection separately from base growth or decay.
lessons.acceptance: Four required questions cover model classification, exact factor/prediction, and shifted/reflected domains, ranges, asymptotes, and direction. Existing exponent rules are reused under separate F05 IDs.

lessons.title: Logarithms reverse exponentials
lessons.objective: Use exponential and logarithmic inverse relationships to evaluate exact values, enforce valid bases and positive arguments, and interpret logarithmic graph features.
scope: b^y=x if and only if log_b(x)=y
Bases b>0 and b!=1, arguments x>0
Common and natural logarithms with explicitly named bases
Negative and fractional logarithmic outputs
Original argument inequalities including products
Reflected inverse points, shifted logarithm domains/ranges/asymptotes
workedExamples: Evaluate log_4(1/8)=-3/2 by an exact power relation
Distinguish an invalid logarithm of zero from a valid logarithm equal to zero
For ln(7-2x), solve x<7/2 with the boundary excluded
For log((x-1)(x+3)), keep both intervals (-infinity,-3) and (1,infinity)
Reflect the exponential point (3,8) to the logarithmic point (8,3)
For log_2(x+2)-1 identify asymptote -2, domain (-2,infinity), range R, and zero at x=0
lessons.guided: Recover the exponent in log_3(1/27), check two proposed bases, and state the domain of ln(5-x).

interaction.purpose: Select a valid base, enter a positive argument, and predict its logarithm. Compare inverse point pairs and a labeled graph/table; reject zero, negative arguments, base one, and invalid typed input clearly.

mistakes: Divide the argument by the base
Misread logarithm as a quotient
Rewrite the statement as base raised to exponent equals argument.
Reject a negative output
Confuse output sign with input positivity
A positive argument below one can have a negative logarithm.
Include the zero-argument boundary
Reuse square-root rather than logarithm domain rules
Require strict positivity before evaluating.
Assume every product factor is positive
Replace a positive product with individual log domains
Use a sign chart for the original product.
lessons.acceptance: Checkpoint questions include exact fractional inverse meaning with base validity, a negative affine argument, a product domain, and reflected logarithmic graph features.

lessons.title: Log rules and equations with domain checks
lessons.objective: Apply logarithm rules on their original domains and solve like-base, general exponential, and logarithmic equations while checking every candidate.
scope: Product, quotient, and power rules with positivity assumptions
Condensing and expanding exact coefficients
ln(x²)=2ln|x| on x!=0 versus 2ln(x) on x>0
Counterexamples to an invented sum rule
Change of base in the correct order
Like-base and general exponential equations
Original log domains, extraneous roots, and no-solution equations
workedExamples: Expand log_2(x^3 sqrt(y)/z^2) for positive x,y,z into coefficients 3,1/2,-2
At x=-3 compare ln(x²), 2ln|x|, and undefined 2ln(x)
Use ln(2+3)=ln5 versus ln2+ln3=ln6 as a counterexample
Solve 5^(2x-1)=125 to get x=2
Solve 3^(2x+1)=7 as (ln7/ln3-1)/2 before rounding
For ln(x-1)+ln(x-4)=ln18, generate -2 and 7 and retain only 7 on x>4
For ln(x+3)-ln(x-1)=ln2 retain x=5 and the original domain x>1
Recognize ln(x-1)=ln(x-3) has no solution on x>3
Evaluate log_5(12) using ln12/ln5 and verify with a power
lessons.guided: Expand a product/quotient with given positive variables, then audit a candidate that violates one original logarithm argument.

interaction.purpose: Choose a proposed identity, predict whether it preserves the full stated domain, and test inputs. Contrast a true quotient rule with a sum-rule counterexample and the negative-input failure of 2ln(x).

mistakes: Split a sum inside a logarithm
Apply a product law to addition
Substitute a simple positive counterexample and compare the arguments.
Lose negative inputs in an even-power rule
Forget the absolute value
Compare the original and rewritten domains explicitly.
Invert the change-of-base quotient
Confuse base and argument
Use ln(argument)/ln(base) and raise the base to the resulting exponent.
Accept every quadratic candidate
Forget the original logs
Check every original argument is strictly positive before retaining a root.
Round intermediate logarithms
Lose accuracy during inversion
Keep the exact logarithmic form until the requested final rounding.
lessons.acceptance: Independent questions combine rule coefficients and domain/invalid-rule judgments, an exact-expression choice with a numerical general-exponential root, a complete domain-filtered log root set, and change-of-base verification. No general expression-evaluation or grading redesign is needed.

lessons.title: Growth, decay, and threshold times
lessons.objective: Fit exponential models, relate discrete factors to continuous rates, and determine doubling, half-life, and threshold times with correct units and model limits.
scope: Two-point fitting with positive data and known model form
Time-step factors versus per-unit rates
A*b^(t/Delta) and A*exp(k*t), with k=ln(b)/Delta
Doubling time, half-life, and time constant distinctions
Supplied voltage-decay models without assuming circuit theory
Nonnegative time domains and reachable thresholds
Zero, initial-value, past-only, and constant-model cases
workedExamples: Fit (1 s,15) and (3 s,60) to A*2^t with A=15/2
A quantity halves every 4 s: use (1/2)^(t/4) and k=-ln2/4 per second
In V(t)=12exp(-t/3), reach 3 V at 3ln4 seconds and verify substitution
Compare tau=3 s with half-life 3ln2 s; one time constant leaves 1/e of the initial value
A continuous growth rate 0.08 per second gives doubling time ln2/0.08
Convert a 5 percent step increase to continuous rate ln(1.05) per step
Explain why a decaying positive model reaches its initial value at t=0, never reaches exact zero at finite t, and cannot reach a larger target for t>=0
Handle a constant model separately: an equal target is attained at every time, another target never
lessons.guided: Recover a decay rate and find a threshold time from a supplied model, keeping the ratio and exponent dimensionless.

interaction.purpose: Choose a time constant, initial value, and target fraction. Predict finite/immediate/unreachable behavior and any finite threshold time, then compare the curve, positive samples, and threshold line.

mistakes: Treat a two-second factor as a one-second factor
Ignore the sampling interval
Write t/Delta explicitly or solve the root for a per-unit factor.
Use the percentage as the continuous rate
Confuse b with ln(b)
Check that exp(k*Delta)=b.
Drop the negative decay sign
Divide logs without a magnitude estimate
A smaller positive threshold after t=0 requires positive elapsed time.
Report a finite zero or negative context time
Ignore the time domain and asymptote
Classify reachability before solving and substitute into the original model.
Call the time constant the half-life
Confuse 1/e with 1/2
At tau the remaining fraction is 1/e; at tau ln2 it is 1/2.
lessons.acceptance: Checkpoint coverage includes fitting, both doubling and half-life, a finite threshold plus immediate/unreachable classifications, and discrete/continuous conversion with units. Tests independently substitute every computed time and handle k=0 explicitly.

lessons.title: Decibels, ratios, and references
lessons.objective: Convert between decibel levels and physical ratios, preserve the reference, and distinguish power addition, cascaded gains, and voltage-based power comparisons.
scope: 10 log10(P/P0) and its inverse
Zero dB and negative levels with positive ratios
Explicit same-unit positive reference quantities
20 log10 amplitude ratio and the squared-power condition
Power gain from RMS voltage using supplied P=V²/R and equal or unequal positive resistance
Cascaded ratios multiply while dB gains add
Independent powers add in linear units, not by adding their individual levels
Zero or negative log arguments have no finite real level
workedExamples: 20 mW relative to 5 mW gives ratio 4 and about 6.0206 dB
A level of -15 dB gives power ratio 10^(-1.5), a positive ratio below one
At equal resistance, voltage ratio 3 gives power ratio 9 and about 9.5424 dB
For output/input voltage ratio 2 with input resistance 50 ohms and output resistance 100 ohms, power ratio is 2 and power gain about 3.0103 dB
Cascaded power factors 10 and 1/10 give net factor 1 and 0 dB
Two independent 1 mW powers sum to 2 mW, about 3.0103 dB relative to 1 mW
Distinguish zero dB from zero power and explain why a reference must be stated
lessons.guided: Convert a power ratio to dB, then compare a voltage-based power calculation with explicitly supplied equal resistances.

interaction.purpose: Change positive input/output powers or RMS voltages and resistances. Predict the physical power ratio and dB gain, compare equal versus unequal resistance, and inspect a ratio-to-level table.

mistakes: Interpret negative dB as negative power
Confuse a logarithm's sign with its input
A positive ratio below one produces a negative logarithm.
Use 20 for every power comparison
Confuse amplitude and power
Start from the requested power ratio; use the square relationship only when established.
Ignore different resistances in a power-gain calculation
Assume equal proportionality constants
Use (Vout/Vin)^2*(Rin/Rout) for the supplied resistive model.
Add independent power levels in dB
Confuse a cascade with a sum
Convert to linear powers, add, then take the logarithm.
Drop units or reference values inside a logarithm
Treat a dimensional value as a ratio
Divide comparable quantities in matching units first.
lessons.acceptance: Required questions cover forward/inverse power ratios with references, unequal-resistance voltage-based power gain, cascade versus power addition, and finite-log domain and zero-level interpretation. Every physics relationship is supplied.
